content:
Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is facing renewed questions about her past statements on a state income tax following her victory over Republican Governor Greg Abbott in the November 3 election, even as she insists she has no plans to introduce one.

The questions center on two points from her record. In a 2016 interview with KXAN, Hinojosa said Texas relied too heavily on property taxes because the state lacked what she called "the third leg of that stool" — income taxes. And in May 2019, as a state representative, she voted against House Joint Resolution 38, a proposed constitutional amendment prohibiting an individual state income tax. The measure passed the Texas House 100–42 and was approved by voters that November.

Laredo State Representative Richard Raymond was among the lawmakers who backed the amendment — he coauthored it and urged his colleagues on the House floor to vote for it.

Hinojosa maintains that she does not support a state income tax and says she never has. She has said her 2019 vote was against repealing an existing ban, a characterization CBS News Texas reported is not supported by the legislative record. Her vote against the amendment did not itself impose or create an income tax.

Sources: Hammrod News Laredo TX; CBS News Texas; Texas Legislative Reference Library; Texas House Journal.

excerpt: Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa faces renewed questions about a 2016 interview in which she described an income tax as a missing "third leg" of Texas taxation, and her 2019 vote against the constitutional amendment banning one. She maintains she does not support a state income tax.
title: Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa Faces Renewed Questions Over Past Income Tax Comments and 2019 Vote
